title: Learn to Cross-Country Ski
subtitle: What the sport is, what to wear, how the techniques fit together, how snow works, and how to share a trail. Six short chapters, free.
meta_description: A free guide to cross-country skiing: classic vs skate, gear and clothing, your first hour on snow, the athletic stance, every classic and skate technique and when to use it, how snow and wax work, and trail etiquette.

course_offer.title: The course
course_offer.lead: This guide tells you what each technique is and when to use it. The course teaches you to do them.
items: The classic module covers diagonal stride, double pole and kick double pole, herringbone and downhills.
The skate module covers free skate, V1 and its climbing variations, V2 and V2 alternate.
Every technique lesson covers body position, timing, where the power comes from, the common errors and the drills that fix them, with filmed demos.
The basics lessons come with either module.

chapters.title: What XC Skiing Is
chapters.subtitle: Two sports on the same snow, and where to find some

sections.title: Two sports on the same snow

blocks.content:
Cross-country skiing is moving yourself across snow on long, skinny skis, under your own power, uphill as well as down. There's no lift. You climb every meter you descend.

It's really two sports that share a trail. Classic skiing keeps your skis parallel in two grooves cut into the snow, and it grips because the middle of the ski presses into the snow when you kick. Skate skiing pushes off the inside edge of one ski and glides on the other, like an ice skater, on a wide, smooth lane beside the tracks. Different skis, boots, poles and motion.

tabs.label: Classic
tabs.content:
Skis stay parallel in set tracks. Grip comes from a kick zone under your foot, either waxed or textured (waxless). The motion is closest to walking or running, which is why I'd start almost everyone here.

The skis are longer, the poles reach about your armpit and the boots are soft and flexible.

tabs.label: Skate
tabs.content:
Skis push out in a V on a wide, groomed lane. There's no kick zone; the whole base is smooth and you push off the edge. It's faster on good snow and harder to learn, mostly because balancing on one gliding ski is the whole game.

The skis are shorter, the poles reach your chin or nose and the boots are stiffer, with a higher cuff.

blocks.title: Start with classic
blocks.content: The motion is closer to walking, it forgives more and most rental fleets are mostly classic. Learn to glide in the tracks, then rent skate skis for a day and find out how humbling balance can be.

In another life I roller skied endless miles trying to be a fast cross-country ski racer. I never became one. A friend of mine had been skiing in Minnesota since he was tiny, didn't go to all the ski camps, and still showed up to every race and beat me.

If you've never skied, you can't jump into a ski race and beat people on fitness alone, however fit you are. Technique is a second engine, and a skier with modest fitness and clean technique glides right past a stronger athlete who's fighting the snow.

Technique is learnable, and most of it comes down to three fundamentals in chapter 3.

You need a groomed trail and, usually, a day pass. Nordic centers sell them, and plenty of state parks, city parks and golf courses groom trails for free.

Start close. The best trail is the one you'll drive to on a Tuesday. A famous Nordic center three hours away does nothing for your skiing if you get there twice a season.

blocks.title: How to find trails near you

steps.title: Search the map
steps.content: Search "Nordic center near me" or "cross-country ski trails" and your town. Most centers have a website with a trail map and pass prices.

steps.title: Check the skier-run listings
steps.content: skinnyski.com and xcskiworld.com both list Nordic trails by state and region.

steps.title: Call your parks department
steps.content: Many city and county parks groom trails in winter and barely mention it. One phone call can turn up a trail ten minutes from home.

steps.title: Ask a ski shop
steps.content: The people at a Nordic shop know which trails are groomed well and which aren't worth the drive.

steps.title: Look at golf courses
steps.content: Flat, open and sometimes groomed in winter. Good beginner terrain that people forget to check.

cards.back: Easy. Flat terrain, gentle slopes, wide trails. Where you start, and there's no need to leave if green trails are what you enjoy.
Intermediate. Moderate hills, some sharper turns. You need to control your speed on the descents and keep your momentum on the climbs.
Difficult. Steep climbs, fast descents, narrow trails and tight turns. You need a snowplow, step turns and a tuck you trust.
Expert only. The steepest, fastest and most technical terrain at the center. If you're reading this guide, these can wait.

blocks.content:
Grooming is how a trail gets made. A machine, usually a snowcat or a snowmobile pulling a drag, packs, tills and smooths the snow. For classic it cuts two parallel tracks. For skate it leaves a wide surface of fine ridges called corduroy.

Good grooming is fresh corduroy, firm and smooth, and classic tracks deep enough to hold your ski without wobbling. Rocks, grass, dirt or icy chunks mean conditions are marginal.

Most Nordic centers post a grooming report every morning on their website or social pages, and some post to apps like Nordic Pulse. Check the timestamp. A report from 6 AM today is useful; one from three days ago tells you almost nothing. If there's no report, call. A short call beats a long drive to bad snow.

blocks.question: You're brand new and heading to a Nordic center for the first time. Which skis do you rent?

options.label: Classic skis, because the motion is closer to walking
options.response: Classic. The motion is close to walking, and most rental fleets are mostly classic.

options.label: It doesn't matter, they're the same

chapters.title: Your First Day
chapters.subtitle: Gear, clothes, and the first hour on snow

blocks.content: Rent for your first three to five outings. Most Nordic centers rent a package of skis, boots and poles by the day, and renting lets you try both classic and skate before you spend real money.

tabs.label: Skis
tabs.content: Classic and skate skis are not interchangeable. Classic skis are longer, roughly your height plus 20 to 25 cm, with a kick zone under the foot. Skate skis are roughly your height plus 10 to 15 cm, with a fully smooth base. Rental staff size them for you.

tabs.label: Boots and bindings
tabs.content:
XC boots look more like sneakers than downhill boots. They clip in only at the toe, so your heel lifts freely. NNN, Prolink and Turnamic boots fit each other's bindings; old SNS boots fit none of them. When you rent, the shop matches them for you.

Classic boots are soft with a low cuff. Skate boots are stiffer with a higher cuff for side-to-side support. Wear one pair of thin socks. You want to feel the ski.

tabs.label: Poles
tabs.content: Classic poles reach about your armpit. Skate poles are taller, chin to nose. Slide your hand up through the strap from below, then grip the handle, so the strap holds your wrist. You push through the strap, not by squeezing the grip.

tabs.label: Waxable or waxless
tabs.content:
Classic only; skate skis have no kick zone. Waxless skis grip with a textured pattern or a mohair skin under the foot and need no kick wax. Waxable skis grip with wax matched to the snow temperature. They ski better and take knowledge and time.

Start waxless. Learn to wax later, if ever. Chapter 5 covers what wax does.

blocks.content: Cross-country skiing makes far more heat than you expect, so dress as if it's 10 to 15°F warmer than it is. If it's 20°F, dress for 30 to 35°F. You'll start a little cold and be warm within a few minutes.

items.title: Base layer
items.content: Synthetic or merino against your skin, never cotton. Cotton soaks up sweat, stays wet and makes you cold the moment you stop.

items.title: Mid layer
items.content: A light fleece or softshell. Skip it above about 25°F, or if you run hot.

items.title: Outer layer
items.content: A light wind jacket or vest you can stuff in a pocket. A full waterproof shell is usually overkill and traps heat.

items.title: Hands, head and eyes
items.content: Light gloves or lobster mitts, plus a dry spare pair. A thin hat or headband, a buff for cold days, and sunglasses. Snow glare is intense on a sunny day.

blocks.title: The classic beginner mistake
blocks.content: Overdressing. If you're warm standing in the parking lot, you'll be soaked ten minutes into the ski and cold the first time you stop.
Your first outing is for getting comfortable. Speed and form can wait. What you want from day one is balance, the feeling of gliding and the ability to stop before you meet a downhill.

steps.title: Gear up (5 min)
steps.content: Set the skis flat and parallel, step into the toe piece until it clicks, and lift your heel to check it hinges at the toe. Hands up through the straps.

steps.title: Shuffle (10 min)
steps.content: On flat ground, slide one ski forward, then the other. Don't try to glide yet. Turn by stepping the tips around like a clock hand.

steps.title: Find a glide (15 min)
steps.content: Push gently off one foot and ride the other. Half a second of glide counts. Let your arms swing like you're walking.

steps.title: Fall and get up (10 min)
steps.content: Sit down to one side, onto your hip, not your hands. To get up, roll so your skis are parallel and below you, tuck your knees, plant both poles together beside your hip and push up sideways. Do it three or four times on purpose. Once you know you can get up, falling stops being scary.

steps.title: Learn to stop (10 min)
steps.content: On the gentlest slope you can find, push the tails apart and bring the tips together into a wedge, the snowplow. Bend your knees and press on the inside edges. Slide a few meters and wedge to a stop. Repeat until you can stop where you choose, every time.

steps.title: Explore (10 min)
steps.content: Ski a green trail at whatever pace feels good. Only ski a downhill you could already stop on. If a hill looks steeper than anything you've stopped on, take your skis off and walk down the side.

blocks.title: A good first day
blocks.content: If you shuffled, glided for a second, got yourself up from a fall and stopped with a snowplow, the day went well. Everything else in skiing is built on those four things.

Keep your first outings to 30 to 60 minutes. Tell someone where you're going, carry your phone in an inside pocket so the battery stays warm, and bring water and a snack. You still sweat in cold, dry air.

Wind chill matters more than the thermometer, and your own speed adds wind. At 20°F with a 15 mph wind the wind chill is about 6°F. FIS won't start a race when the coldest point on the course is below -20°C (-4°F). Use that as your limit too, then check the wind chill on top of it.

Frostbite turns skin white or waxy and numb. Get inside, warm it with body heat or warm (not hot) water, never rub it, and see a doctor. Shivering, confusion and clumsy hands are early hypothermia. Go in.

Skip whiteouts, when you can't see trail markers or other skiers, and the sheet ice that follows rain and a freeze. Wait for fresh grooming.

chapters.title: The Foundation
chapters.subtitle: Stance, weight transfer, hips, and how you get better

blocks.content: Classic or skate, uphill or down, every technique rests on an athletic stance, full weight transfer and high, forward hips. When a skier looks effortless, it's usually these three. When a skier is working hard and going nowhere, it's usually these three too.

Stand like you're about to jump. Ankles bent, knees bent, hips forward, weight on the balls of your feet, shoulders relaxed, arms hanging. You come back to this position between every movement on skis.

blocks.title: Find it in ten seconds
blocks.content: Jump straight up on flat ground and notice how your body loads right before takeoff. That's the stance.

This is the biggest difference between a struggling beginner and a competent skier. Whenever you glide on one ski, all of your weight goes over that ski, not most of it. (Double poling is the exception; both skis share your weight.)

New skiers keep their weight between their skis because it feels safe. Split weight means neither ski has enough pressure to glide, so you shuffle. Getting your hip over one ski feels like you're about to fall over. Commit anyway. That falling feeling is what weight transfer feels like.

blocks.title: Find it in ten seconds
blocks.content: Stand on one foot and hop. Your hip is right over that foot. That's where it belongs on every one-ski glide.

With your hips high and forward, your body weight presses the ski into the snow, and that pressure is your glide and your grip. With your hips back, your legs have to make up the difference on every stride, spending energy on work your body weight would have done for free.

The right position feels wrong for a while. If you feel comfortable, your hips are probably too far back.

More kilometers of the same mistakes make you very good at the mistakes. You get better through a loop: try one thing, get feedback, adjust, repeat.

Expect a long, annoying stretch where you know what good looks like and can't do it yet. That's where most people quit, and it's where practice pays off most.

steps.title: Pick one thing
steps.content: One focus per session, and a specific one: "hips forward" or "all my weight on the glide ski", never "ski better".

steps.title: Go slowly
steps.content: If you can't do it slowly, you can't do it fast.

steps.title: Get feedback
steps.content: Have a friend film you from the side and from behind. Then ask yourself the plain questions. Were my hips forward? Did I commit to one ski?

steps.title: Change one thing and repeat
steps.content: When it feels easy and automatic, move on to the next thing.

blocks.title: Practice where falling is cheap
blocks.content: Flat ground, soft snow, nobody behind you. If you never fall while you're practicing a new position, you're not really trying the new position.

blocks.question: You're gliding on your right ski. Where should your weight be?

options.label: Split evenly between both skis, for balance
All of it on the right ski, hip over the foot
options.response: All of it. Split weight means neither ski has the pressure to glide.

chapters.title: The Gears
chapters.subtitle: Every classic and skate technique, and when to shift

blocks.content:
Picking the right technique for the terrain matters more than how pretty any one technique looks. A beautiful diagonal stride on a fast flat, where double poling is quicker, costs you time and energy.

If you ride a bike, you already know this. You don't grind up a hill in your biggest gear or spin 130 rpm on a flat. You shift. Skiing works the same way, except the gears are whole techniques.

blocks.title: Classic, from flat to steep
rows: Flats and gentle downhills on fast snow
Both poles plant together and you drive your body weight down through them. Your upper body and core do the work and your legs get a break.
Rolling terrain, gentle climbs, slow snow
One kick, then a double pole. The kick carries you further between pole plants when double poling alone runs out of steam.
Opposite arm, opposite leg, like walking or running. The kick presses the grip zone into the snow, and you glide on the other ski.
Tips out in a V, skis on their inside edges, and walk up. Slow, ugly, and it works. Fast skiers herringbone the steepest pitches too.
Low and still, and only on a hill you can already stop on.

blocks.content: There's one more classic gear, the Klaebo step, named for the Norwegian sprinter who made it famous. It's a quick, running diagonal stride with very little glide, for short, steep pitches.
The skate names (V1, V2, V2 alternate) confuse everyone, so tie each one to the terrain rather than memorizing the name. Mostly they differ in when your poles go in.

blocks.title: Skate, from flat to steep
rows: No poles. Push off one ski's edge and glide on the other, arms swinging for balance.
One double pole for every two skate pushes. The gear you can hold for a long time.
A double pole with every skate push. Faster to get up to speed, harder to sustain.
One pole plant for every two skate pushes, both poles planting together as you step onto one side. The main skate climbing gear. On steeper pitches, shorten everything and pick up the tempo.

blocks.content: Grade is the obvious reason to change gears. These matter as much.

items.title: Fatigue
items.content: Fresh legs at kilometer 2 can hold V2 on the flats and double pole the gentle rises. Tired legs at kilometer 25 should drop a gear. Forcing a gear you no longer have the energy for wrecks your form and buys less speed for more effort.

items.title: Snow
items.content: Slow, wet snow punishes the bigger gears, so add a kick to your double pole, and on skate skis shift down sooner. Cold, fast snow lets you hold the bigger gears longer.

items.title: Trail width
items.content: Skating needs room. On a narrow trail, shorten your pushes and narrow the V. Narrower still, double pole until it opens up.

items.title: Racing
items.content: Behind someone on a flat, match their gear and don't overwork. To get away on a climb, shift up long enough to break contact, then settle back. A better tuck on a descent opens a gap for free.

blocks.title: When in doubt, shift down
blocks.content: Smooth in an easier technique beats ragged in a harder one. A sloppy V2 is slower than a clean V2 alternate, and a struggling double pole is slower than a solid kick double pole.

Shift a few meters before the terrain changes, not once you're already struggling. Look ahead, see the hill coming and let the last stroke of one technique set up the first stroke of the next.

The best way I know to learn this is a rolling trail at easy effort, thinking only about the transitions. Double pole to kick double pole on the rise, back to double pole on the flat, tuck on the descent. Half an hour of that teaches more about choosing gears than an hour of hammering one technique.

blocks.question: You're skating, your form is falling apart and you're breathing hard. What do you do?

options.label: Push harder to hold the speed
Shift down to an easier technique and clean it up
options.response: Shift down. Clean form in an easier gear is faster than sloppy form in a hard one.

options.label: Stop until you can hold the technique again

chapters.title: How Snow Works
chapters.subtitle: Temperature, wax, and checking conditions before you drive

blocks.content: Temperature and the shape of the snow crystals decide how fast you glide, how well you grip and whether your wax works. You don't need a meteorology degree. Four zones cover nearly every day you'll ski.

tabs.label: Cold and dry (below 15°F)
tabs.content: Squeaky underfoot, and the skis feel slow, almost sticky. The crystals are sharp and there's very little moisture to make a glide layer, so friction is high. Grip is excellent. Cold kick waxes (green, blue) work, and so do waxless skis. You'll work harder for less speed. Cover your skin.

tabs.label: The sweet spot (15 to 30°F)
tabs.content: Fast and smooth. There's enough moisture for a thin water film under the ski and the snow is still firm. Good glide, good grip, and everything feels crisp. Pick the kick wax whose printed range matches the day.

tabs.label: Warm and wet (above 30°F)
tabs.content: Heavy and draggy, and you'll sweat more than you expect. Free water sits on the surface and the crystals round off. Hard kick wax stops gripping, so classic skiers need klister or waxless skis. Skate holds up better than classic. Go early, before the sun softens everything further.

tabs.label: Spring corn
tabs.content: Frozen overnight, crunchy at dawn, fast and forgiving by mid-morning, slush by afternoon. Timing decides the day. Bring sunscreen; spring sun off snow burns fast. Skip hard kick wax: go waxless, or use klister if you're feeling brave.

blocks.content: Wax scares a lot of new skiers. For your first season you need to know four things.

items.title: Kick wax
items.content: Goes on the middle of a classic ski, the grip zone. It's sticky enough to grip when you press down and slippery enough to glide when you don't. Every kick wax has a temperature range printed on it. Follow the chart, rub it on, cork it smooth. Five minutes once you've done it a few times.

items.title: Glide wax
items.content: Goes on the whole base of a skate ski and on the tips and tails of a classic ski, to make it slide. You iron it on, let it cool and scrape it off. Most beginners have a shop do it or use a rub-on or spray-on. Use fluoro-free wax; FIS banned fluorinated wax from the 2023/24 season.

items.title: Why waxless skis exist
items.content: They grip with fish scales or a mohair skin and need no kick wax. They're slower than a well-waxed ski and always ready: no temperature guessing, no wax box, no 20 minutes in a cold garage. For your first season, and for plenty of skiers after that, they're the right ski.

items.title: When to start waxing
items.content: When you're skiing two or three times a week and can feel the difference between a good snow day and a bad one. When you're racing. Or when you want a project, because some people love the ritual. Don't rush it. A mediocre skier on perfect wax is still a mediocre skier.

steps.title: Temperature and its trend
steps.content: Where the temperature is going matters more than the forecast high. Warming means the snow gets worse as you ski. Cooling means it firms up later. Fresh snow falling during your ski is beautiful and slow.

steps.title: The grooming report
steps.content: Which trails were groomed, when, and any notes. Today's timestamp or it doesn't count. No report, call.

steps.title: Wind chill
steps.content: At 15°F with a 15 mph wind it's about 0°F on your face, and your own speed adds more. The National Weather Service chart puts frostbite on exposed skin at about 30 minutes once the wind chill reaches about -19°F. Below about -20°F, think about staying home.

steps.title: Classic or skate
steps.content: Warm and slushy favors skate. Cold with good tracks is a classic day. Icy favors skate, which gives you more control on the wide lane. If no classic tracks are set, leave the classic skis at home.

blocks.question: It's 35°F and sunny and you're going classic skiing. What's the problem?

options.label: Too cold for the kick wax to work
Hard kick wax won't grip the wet snow
options.response: Warm, wet snow is the classic skier's problem day. Use klister or waxless skis.

options.label: The snow is too dry to glide

chapters.title: Trail Etiquette
chapters.subtitle: How to share a trail, safety first

blocks.content: Nobody likes the skier who snowplows down the middle of the classic tracks, stops on a blind corner and has music so loud they never hear "on your left". Etiquette comes down to one idea: pay attention to the people around you. The safety rules come first, because a collision hurts people. Everything else is manners.

steps.title: Let faster skiers by
steps.content: Move over enough to give them a clean line. You don't have to dive into a snowbank. The passing skier is responsible for passing safely, and on a hill the skier coming down has priority over the skier going up, because they can't stop as easily.

steps.title: Say it when you pass
steps.content: "On your left" or "track", loud enough and early enough not to startle anyone. Then don't pass and slow down in front of them. That's brake-checking on skis.

steps.title: Stop off the trail
steps.content: Never in the middle, never on a blind corner, never right over a crest. If you fall, get up and move to the side before you catch your breath.

steps.title: Give groomers the whole trail
steps.content: They weigh several tons and can't swerve. Get completely off the trail and wait for the driver to wave you on.

steps.title: Ski your level
steps.content: If you can't stop on a hill with a snowplow, that hill is above your level today. A beginner snowplowing down a black diamond forces everyone behind them to brake or bail.

steps.title: Stay out of the classic tracks
steps.content: On skate skis, or on foot, stay out of the set tracks. One careless skater can wreck a long stretch, and nothing fixes it until the groomer comes back, which may be tomorrow.

steps.title: Ask before you draft
steps.content: Skiing two feet behind a stranger in the woods is unsettling, whatever the sport. Ask. Most people say yes.

steps.title: Leave no trace
steps.content: Pack out every gel wrapper. Don't ski where the snow is so thin you're on dirt and plants. If dogs are allowed and you bring one, clean up after it.

blocks.title: Keep one ear free
blocks.content: You need to hear "on your left", a groomer coming and the wildlife. Moose don't announce themselves. Bone-conduction headphones leave your ears open.
You'll break one of these eventually. Everyone has stepped in the tracks, stopped in a bad spot or missed someone calling a pass. Say sorry, wave and fix it.

blocks.question: Which of these is the most serious?

options.label: Walking in the set classic tracks
Stopping in the track right below a blind corner on a descent
options.response: Safety comes first. The skier coming down can't see you in time to stop. Walking in the tracks is still wrong, but it doesn't put anyone in danger.

options.label: Following a stranger closely without asking
